A '''Synergistic system''' (or '''S-system''')<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Savageau |first=Michael A. |date=1988-01-01 |title=Introduction to S-systems and the underlying power-law formalism |journal=Mathematical and Computer Modelling |volume=11 |pages=546–551 |doi=10.1016/0895-7177(88)90553-5 |issn=0895-7177|doi-access=free }}</ref> is a collection of ordinary [[Non-linear differential equations|nonlinear differential equations]]

<math>\frac{dx_i}{dt}= \alpha_{i} \prod_{j=1}^{n+m} x_i ^{g_{ij}}- \beta_{j} \prod_{j=1}^{n+m} x_i ^{h_{ij}}  ~~~~~  (i=1,...,n)</math>

where the <math>x_{i}</math> are positive real, <math>\alpha_{i}</math> and <math>\beta_{i}</math> are non-negative real, called the '''[[Reaction rate constant|rate constant]]'''(or, '''kinetic rates''') and <math>g_{ij}</math> and <math>h_{ij}</math> are real exponential, called '''kinetic orders'''. These terms are based on the [[chemical equilibrium]]'''<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Tournier |first=Laurent |chapter=Approximation of dynamical systems using s-systems theory: Application to biological systems |date=2005-07-24 |title=Proceedings of the 2005 international symposium on Symbolic and algebraic computation |chapter-url=https://doi.org/10.1145/1073884.1073928 |series=ISSAC '05 |location=New York, NY, USA |publisher=Association for Computing Machinery |pages=317–324 |doi=10.1145/1073884.1073928 |isbn=978-1-59593-095-8|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref>'''

== One variable S-system ==
Source:<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Savageau |first=Michael A. |title=Biochemical systems analysis: a study of function and design in molecular biology |last2=Rosen |first2=Robert |date=1976 |publisher=Addison-Wesley |isbn=978-0-201-06738-5 |edition=40th Anniversary |series=Advanced book program |location=London}}</ref>

In the case of <math>n=1 (i=1)</math> and <math>m=0</math>, the given S-system equation can be written as

<math>\ \frac{dx}{dt}= \alpha x^{g}-\beta x^{h} \     </math>

Under the non-zero steady condition, <math>\frac{dx_0}{dt}= 0</math>,  the following non-linear equation can be transformed into an [[ordinary differential equation]](ODE).

'''Transformation one variable S-system into a first-order ODE'''

Let <math>x=e^{\operatorname{log} x}=e^{y}</math>(with <math>x_0=e^{y_0}</math>)  Then, given a one-variable S-system is

<math>\frac{dy}{dt}=\alpha e^{(g-1)y}-\beta e^{(h-1)y}</math>

Apply a non-zero steady condition to the given equation

<math>0=\frac{dy_{0}}{dt}=\alpha e^{(g-1)y_{0}}-\beta e^{(h-1)y_{0}}</math>, or equivalently  <math>\alpha e^{(g-1)y_{0}}=\beta e^{(h-1)y_{0}}</math>

Thus,  <math>y_0 = \frac{\operatorname{log}\beta-\operatorname{log}\alpha}{g-h}</math>(or,  <math>x_0 = \left(\frac{\beta}{\alpha}\right)^{\frac{1}{g-h}}</math>)

If  <math>\frac{dy}{dt}</math> can be approximated around <math>y=y_0</math>, remaining the first two terms,

<math>\frac{dy}{dt} \simeq  \alpha e^{(g-1)y_0}+\alpha e^{(g-1)y_0}(g-1)(y-y_{0})-\beta e^{(g-1)y_0} - \beta  e^{(h-1)y_0}(h-1)(y-y_{0})</math>

By non-zero steady condition, <math>\alpha e^{(g-1)y_{0}}=\beta e^{(h-1)y_{0}}</math>, a nonlinear one-variable S-system can be transformed into [[First-order ordinary differential equation|a first-order ODE]]:

<math>\frac{du}{dt} \simeq \left ( \alpha e^{(g-1)y_0} (g-h) \right )u= \left ( Fa \right )u</math>

where  <math>F=\alpha e^{(g-1)y_0}</math>,  <math>a=g-h</math>, and   <math>u=y-y_0 \simeq \frac{x-x_0}{x_0} </math>, called a '''percentage variation'''.

== Two variables S-system ==
Source:<ref name=":1" />

In the case of <math>n=2 (i=1,2)</math> and <math>m=0</math> , the S-system equation can be written as [[System of equations|system of (non-linear) differential equations]].

<math>\left\{\begin{matrix}
 \frac{dx_1}{dt}= \alpha_{1}x_{1}^{g_{11}}x_2^{g_{21}}-\beta_{1}x_{1}^{h_{11}}x_{2}^{h_{21}} \ \\
 \frac{dx_2}{dt}= \alpha_{2}x_{2}^{g_{21}}x_2^{g_{22}}-\beta_{2}x_{1}^{h_{21}}x_{2}^{h_{22}}
\end{matrix}\right.     </math>

Assume non-zero steady condition, <math>\frac{dx_{i0}}{dt}= 0    </math>.

'''Transformation two variables S-system into a second-order ODE'''

By putting <math>x_{i}=e^{\operatorname{log} x_{i}}=e^{y_{i}}  </math> . The given system of equations can be written as

<math>\left\{\begin{matrix}
 \frac{d u_{1}}{dt}= c_{11}u_{1}+ c_{12}u_{2}  \ \\
 \frac{d u_{2}}{dt}= c_{21}u_{1}+ c_{22}u_{2}   
\end{matrix}\right.</math>

(where <math>u_{i}=y_{i}-y_{i0}</math>, <math>u_{i}=y_{i}-y_{i0}</math> and <math>c_{ij}(i,j=1,2)</math> are constant.

Since <math>\frac{d^{2}u_{1}}{dt^{2}}=c_{11}\frac{du_{1}}{dt}+c_{12}\frac{du_{2}}{dt}     </math>,  the given system of equation can be approximated as a second-order ODE:

<math>\frac{d^{2}u_{1}}{dt^{2}}-  \left ( c_{11}+c_{22} \right )\frac{du_{1}}{dt}+\left ( c_{11}c_{22}-c_{12}c_{21} \right )u_{1}=0     </math>,

== Applications ==

=== Mass-action Law ===
Source:<ref name=":0" />

Consider the following chemical pathway:

<chem>A + 2B ->[k_1] C ->[k_2]  3D + E   </chem>

where <math>k_{1}</math> and <math>k_{2}</math> are [[Rate constant|rate constants]]. 

Then the [[Law of mass action|mass-action law]] applied to species <chem>C</chem>  gives the equation

<math>\frac{d[C]}{dt}=k_1[A][B]^{2}-k_{2}[D]^{3}[E]</math>

(where <math>[A]</math> is a [[concentration]] of A etc.)

=== Komarova Model ([[Bone remodeling|Bone Remodeling]]) ===
Sources:<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Komarova |first1=Svetlana V. |last2=Smith |first2=Robert J. |last3=Dixon |first3=S. Jeffrey |last4=Sims |first4=Stephen M. |last5=Wahl |first5=Lindi M. |date=August 2003 |title=Mathematical model predicts a critical role for osteoclast autocrine regulation in the control of bone remodeling |journal=Bone |volume=33 |issue=2 |pages=206–215 |doi=10.1016/s8756-3282(03)00157-1 |issn=8756-3282 |pmid=14499354}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ramtani |first1=Salah |last2=Sánchez |first2=Juan Felipe |last3=Boucetta |first3=Abdelkader |last4=Kraft |first4=Reuben |last5=Vaca-González |first5=Juan Jairo |last6=Garzón-Alvarado |first6=Diego A. |date=June 2023 |title=A coupled mathematical model between bone remodeling and tumors: a study of different scenarios using Komarova's model |journal=Biomechanics and Modeling in Mechanobiology |volume=22 |issue=3 |pages=925–945 |doi=10.1007/s10237-023-01689-3 |issn=1617-7940 |pmc=10167202 |pmid=36922421}}</ref>

Komarova Model is an example of a two-variable system of non-linear differential equations that describes [[bone remodeling]]. This equation is regulated by biochemical factors called [[Paracrine signaling|paracrine]] and [[Autocrine signaling|autocrine]], which quantify the bone mass in each step.

<math>\left\{\begin{matrix}
 \quad \frac{dx_{1}}{dt} = \alpha_{1} x_{1}^{g_{11}}x_{2}^{g_{21}}-\beta_{1}x_{1} 
 \\ \quad \frac{dx_{2}}{dt} = \alpha_{2} x_{1}^{g_{12}}x_{2}^{g_{22}}-\beta_{2}x_{2}
 \\ \frac{dz}{dt}= -k_{1}y_{1}+k_{2}y_{2}
\end{matrix}\right.</math>

Where

* <math>x_1</math>, <math>x_2</math>: The number of [[osteoclast]]/[[osteoblast]]s
* <math>\alpha_{1}</math>, <math>\alpha_{2}</math>: Osteoclast/Osteoblast production rate
* <math>\beta_{1}</math>, <math>\beta_{2}</math>: Osteoclast/Osteoblast removal rate
* <math>g_{ij}</math>: Paracrine factor on the <math>j</math>-cell due to the presence of <math>i</math>-cell
* <math>z</math>: [[Bone mass|The bone mass percentage]]
* <math>y_{i}</math>: Let  <math>\bar{x_i}</math> be the difference between the number of osteoclasts/osteoblasts and its steady state. Then  <math>y_{i}:=\frac{1}{2} \left [ \left ( x_{i} - \bar{x_{i}})+(x_{i}-\bar{x_{i}}) \right )  \right ]</math>

=== Modified Komarova Model (Bone Remodeling with Tumor affecting, [[Bone metastasis]]) ===
Source:<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ayati |first1=Bruce P. |last2=Edwards |first2=Claire M. |last3=Webb |first3=Glenn F. |last4=Wikswo |first4=John P. |date=2010-04-20 |title=A mathematical model of bone remodeling dynamics for normal bone cell populations and myeloma bone disease |journal=Biology Direct |volume=5 |pages=28 |doi=10.1186/1745-6150-5-28 |doi-access=free |issn=1745-6150 |pmc=2867965 |pmid=20406449}}</ref>

The modified Komarova Model describes the [[tumor]] effect on the osteoclasts and osteoblasts rate. The following equation can be described as

<math>\left\{\begin{matrix}
 \frac{dx_{1}}{dt} = \widehat{ \alpha_{1}(\omega)}x_{1}^{g_{11}}x_{2}^{g_{21}}-\widehat{\beta_{1}(\omega)}x_{1} 
 \\ \frac{dx_{2}}{dt} = \widehat{ \alpha_{2}(\omega)} x_{2}^{g_{22}}-\widehat{ \beta_{2}(\omega)}x_{2}
 \\ \frac{d\omega}{dt}= \mu \omega \operatorname{log}\left (\sigma \frac{L_{\omega}}{\omega}  \right )
\end{matrix}\right.</math>

(with [[initial condition]] <math>x_1(0)=x_{10}</math>, <math>x_2(0)=x_{20}</math>, and <math>\omega(0)=\omega_{0}</math>)

Where

* <math>x_1</math>, <math>x_2</math>: The number of [[osteoclast]]/[[osteoblast]]s.
* <math>\omega=\omega(t)</math> : The tumor representation depending on time <math>t</math>
* <math>\widehat{\alpha_{1}(\omega)}</math>,<math>\widehat{\alpha_{2}(\omega)}</math>: The representation of the activity of cell production
* <math>\widehat{\beta_{1}(\omega)}</math>,<math>\widehat{\beta_{2}(\omega)}</math>:  The representation of the activity of cell removal
* <math>g_{ij}</math>: The net effectiveness of osteoclast/osteoblast derived autocrine and paracrine factors
* <math>\mu</math> : The tumor cell proliferation rate
* <math>L_{\omega}</math>: The upper limit value for tumor cells
* <math>\sigma</math> : Scaling constant of tumor growth
